headline: IBM and Chicago ran 70 logical qubits — and could prove the answer was right
dek: 2,415 logical two-qubit gates and 468 T gates, at effective error rates about ten times below the physical ones underneath. The new part is not the size. It is that the result is checkable.

source.name: arXiv
source.title: Sampling hard circuits with verifiably high fidelity (arXiv:2607.25941); reported by The Quantum Insider, 31 July 2026

body_html:
A team from IBM and the University of Chicago reported running an encoded circuit on 70 logical qubits, executing 2,415 logical two-qubit operations and 468 logical T gates, in roughly fifteen minutes of machine time. Because the circuit was error-corrected, the effective logical error rate came out about ten times lower than the physical error rate of the hardware carrying it. The circuits were released through the Quantum Advantage Tracker so other groups can benchmark against them.

The number worth holding is not 70. It is the word verifiably in the paper's title. Sampling experiments have always had the same weakness: the output is hard to produce and equally hard to check, so "we did something a classical computer cannot" has historically rested on an argument rather than a receipt. This work is aimed squarely at that gap — producing a hard sampling result whose fidelity can be independently established.

The T-gate count is the second thing to notice. T gates are the expensive ones: Clifford operations alone are classically simulable, so a circuit's difficulty lives in its non-Clifford content, and on a fault-tolerant machine those gates are paid for by magic-state distillation. 468 of them is a real workload, not a demonstration of two.

What this does NOT mean

  • It is not a useful application. The circuit was chosen because it is hard to simulate, not because anyone wants its output. Nothing here schedules a delivery fleet, designs a molecule, or breaks a key.
  • The 10× is not "error-free". It is a comparison between the logical error rate of this encoded circuit and the physical error rate of the qubits underneath it, on this run. It is not a general speedup, and it is not a claim that logical qubits are now reliable in the way a classical bit is.
  • "Beyond classical simulation" is a moving line, not a wall. That boundary is defined by the best classical method anyone has published, and it has moved in both directions before — Google's 2019 Sycamore claim has been matched, beaten, and re‑matched by classical simulation in the years since. A result past today's line can be behind tomorrow's without anybody having done anything wrong.
  • 70 logical qubits here does not mean 70 logical qubits for anything else. Logical qubit counts are quoted for a specific code, a specific circuit and a specific error budget. They do not port.
concept_card_html:
Concepts in this story

Each of these is already explained on SymbiQ. Depth chips say how deep the explanation goes.

  • logical qubitplainOne reliable qubit built out of many unreliable ones. The only qubit count that means anything.
  • quantum error correctionplainSpreading one fragile qubit across many so the machine can find mistakes without ever looking at the answer.
  • magic-state factoriesformalClifford gates alone are classically simulable, so universality is smuggled in via a purified magic state -- consume several noisy copies, distill out fewer higher-fidelity ones.
  • NISQ & quantum advantage experimentsplainNoisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum, the era the field is actually in -- and the still-unsettled tug-of-war between Google's 2019 Sycamore claim and classical simulations that have matched, lost to, and matched it again since.
